notes.key_messages: Candidates should ensure that they read the questions carefully before starting to answer. This is particularly important for any planning exercise that is required. Identification of the dependent and independent variables is vital before a plan is completed. Controlled variables must also be considered and included in a plan. When asked about safety considerations, candidates should identify a risk, but also identify a method of reducing that risk. Mathematical calculations form an important part of the practical assessment. It is essential that candidates check all their working carefully and take time to consider whether the resulting answer is realistic. It is essential that candidates take time to ensure that their written work is legible. This includes the avoidance of ‘overwriting’ when mistakes are made or even writing in pencil and then overwriting in pen. When mistakes are made, they should be crossed out completely and the alternative answer written in a suitable clear space.
notes.general_comments: Most candidates performed well on this paper. Some of the questions relied on a good knowledge of a variety of food tests. It was clear that although most candidates had experience of food testing in a practical context, a large number were less sure of the techniques involved or of the outcomes expected. For the graph question, candidates demonstrated a good ability to plot complex data with good attention to detail. Most candidates have understood the key points when drawing biological specimens, but care should be taken to avoid shading.
notes.1ai: The presentation of data was generally well done with most candidates gaining three or four marks for a well-constructed table and inclusion of suitable data. The most common error was to produce three separate tables, with one for each drink or one for each food test. It is expected that all the results obtained during the practical activity are presented in a single table with over-arching headings.
notes.1aii: For this question, candidates were required to determine the nutrient present in each drink based on the results of the food tests from (a)(i) . A significant number of candidates found this challenging, possibly due to lack of familiarity with the colour changes observed with each food test.
notes.1aiii: The majority of candidates could identify that heating water is a safety hazard associated with doing the test for reducing sugars. A small number of candidates appeared to be unsure what was meant by the term hazard.
notes.1bi: and (ii) Very few candidates could correctly identify the reagent used when testing for vitamin C. Similarly, very few could correctly describe the test for fats using the emulsion method. It is important that candidates are familiar with the full range of food tests and have carried them out in the laboratory.
notes.1biii: and (iv) These questions asked candidates to identify a drink based on results of the vitamin C and fat tests. Slightly more candidates were familiar with the results of a positive test than were with the test itself. Apart from a few candidates who appeared to have guessed the answer, those who correctly identified the drink gave good explanations in (b)(iv) .
notes.1c: This question asked candidates to plan an investigation into the effect of changing the concentration of the enzyme catalase on the production of oxygen gas. Although many candidates could identify the variables that needed to be kept constant and some safety features, very few showed an understanding of how the volume of oxygen could be measured as the dependent variable. The idea of repeated measurements was commonly seen.
notes.2ai: The graph question was well attempted with many candidates able to plot data that had positive and negative values. The axes labels were good, reflecting what was written as column headings in the table. Care needs to be taken when plotting points, with a few candidates assuming that 0.1 on the scale was in fact 0.2. Plotted points must be small points or crosses. Lines of best fit or lines joining points need to be drawn neatly.
notes.2aii: Most candidates were able to state one simple conclusion from the data but far fewer were able to extend this further and go on to give a second conclusion. This was a demanding question, and many candidates gave thoughtful answers.
notes.2aiii: Most candidates could identify the independent variable for this investigation, although a significant number stated the dependent variable instead. It is important that candidates can distinguish between dependent, independent, and controlled variables.
notes.2aiv: Candidates suggested many correct variables that the scientists should have considered when selecting participants for the clinical trial.
notes.2av: For this question candidates were expected to understand that having large numbers of participants in a clinical trial is equivalent to carrying out replicates for an investigation. Some candidates found this demanding.
notes.2avi: Many candidates correctly identified that because a narrow range of people were chosen for the study, it was not representative of the whole population.
notes.2bi: Some of the drawings of the femur were particularly impressive, with excellent proportions and attention to detail. A few candidates produced more of an artistic impression of the bone with lots of shading and texture. Biological drawings should not be shaded. Another relatively common error was to draw the bone too large. The drawing should be at least as large as the original but should not extend into the text of the question or off the page.
notes.2bii: The calculation was done well overall but two common mistakes meant that few gained full marks. Some candidates measured the length of the bone they had drawn rather than the length of PQ on the photograph. Many candidates confused significant figures with decimal places.
notes.2biii: The majority of candidates were able to identify two differences between the bones.
